desc:
A town has n junctions numbered 0 to n - 1. Each entry roads[i] = [a, b, w] is a two-way road between junctions a and b that takes w minutes to drive in either direction. Several roads may join the same pair of junctions, and a road may lead from a junction back to itself.

A courier starts at junction src and may drive for at most budget minutes in total. Return how many junctions the courier can reach, counting the starting junction itself. A junction counts if the fastest route to it takes at most budget minutes.

n = 5, src = 0, budget = 5
roads = [[0,1,4], [1,2,3], [0,3,2], [3,2,1], [3,4,9]]
fastest times: 0 -> 0, 3 -> 2, 2 -> 3, 1 -> 4, 4 -> 11
-> 4 junctions (0, 3, 2 and 1)
hints: A junction counts exactly when its fastest travel time from src is at most budget. So the real task is computing fastest travel times.
Roads have different lengths, so breadth-first search (which counts roads, not minutes) is not enough. Expand junctions in order of increasing travel time using a min-heap of (time, junction).

Run Dijkstra from src. Because times only grow along a route, you can stop as soon as the popped time exceeds budget, or simply never push times above budget. Count each junction the first time it is popped.
editorial: This is Dijkstra's algorithm with an early cut-off. Keep the best known time for every junction and a min-heap of (time, junction) pairs. The first time a junction leaves the heap its time is final, because every road takes a positive number of minutes and so no later route can be shorter.

Since the heap pops times in non-decreasing order, the first popped time that exceeds budget means every remaining junction is out of reach, and we can stop. Each junction that is popped (and not stale) within the budget is counted once. The cost is O((V + E) log E); the cut-off just saves work.
Edge cases: budget = 0 gives 1 (only the start, since every road takes at least a minute); self-loops never help; parallel roads are handled by relaxation, which keeps the faster one.
